summary: Elimelech of Lizhensk (1717-1787), who settled at Lezajsk (Lizhensk) in Galicia, was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, and, with his brother Zusha (Meshulam Zusha) of Anipoli, a key figure in carrying Hasidism into Galicia and southern Poland. He is remembered above all for his book No'am Elimelech ('the Pleasantness of Elimelech'), a commentary on the Torah that is one of the foundational texts of the doctrine of the tzaddik: the account, given as his and the movement's attributed teaching, of the righteous leader (tzaddik) as the channel through whom divine flow (shefa) descends to the community, an emphasis often described by scholars as 'practical' or 'popular' tzaddikism, which helped shape the institution of the Hasidic rebbe. He worked in the period of sharp Mitnagdic opposition to the spreading movement.
description:
Elimelech ben Elazar Lipman, known after his town as Elimelech of Lizhensk (Lezajsk, in Galicia, then in the Habsburg lands, now in Poland) and after his book as the No'am Elimelech, lived 1717-1787. In the account of the Hasidic movement he was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, the principal successor of the Baal Shem Tov, and, together with his brother Meshulam Zusha of Anipoli (Zusha), one of the disciples who carried Hasidism westward into Galicia and southern Poland, a region where he became a central master and where a line of his own disciples continued after him.

His lasting significance in the scholarship and in the tradition alike is as a formulator, in his book No'am Elimelech, of the doctrine of the tzaddik, the righteous one, as the leader of the community. On this teaching, given here as his and the movement's attributed teaching and not as a claim the editor affirms, the tzaddik is the one who, through his cleaving to God, draws down the divine flow (shefa) upon the community and sustains it: in the No'am Elimelech on Bereshit, it is 'the complete clinging that the righteous have, through which they bring down the flow to all Israel', and the tzaddik 'congregates the congregations of Yaakov that are collected under the shadow of the righteous' wings to bestow on them'; in the comment on Noach, the 'complete tzadik arouses Compassion' for the world at the time of its need. Modern scholars, among them Arthur Green and Immanuel Etkes, describe this as the theological basis of what is often called 'practical' or 'popular' tzaddikism, the reading of the righteous leader as an active intermediary of blessing and sustenance for ordinary followers, which they connect to the emergence and social organization of the Hasidic rebbe as an institution; this scholarly characterization of the doctrine's precise contours rests on their studies and is recorded here as such.

No'am Elimelech ('the Pleasantness of Elimelech'), first printed at the end of the eighteenth century, is arranged as a commentary on the weekly Torah portions and is accompanied by short works of counsel, among them the Tzetel Katan ('the little note') of practical spiritual instructions. It is studied within Hasidism as one of the classic and most influential works of the movement's early literature, and the town of Lezajsk became, and remains, a site of pilgrimage associated with him; the pilgrimage tradition is recorded here as the tradition's practice, not adjudicated.

Elimelech worked in the decades when the young Hasidic movement met organized opposition from the mitnagdim, the 'opponents' led from Vilna; the conflict between Hasidim and mitnagdim, and the mitnagdic objection to the elevation of the tzaddik in particular, are recorded here as the historical context of his career and are not adjudicated. This entry presents Elimelech on the tradition's own terms as a disciple of the Maggid, as one of those who brought Hasidism to Galicia with his brother Zusha, and as the author of No'am Elimelech and a formulator of the doctrine of the tzaddik, with that doctrine attributed to him and to the movement and the scholarship recorded alongside.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Elimelech of Lizhensk on Judaism's own terms as a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch, one of the disciples (with his brother Zusha of Anipoli) who spread Hasidism into Galicia, and the author of No'am Elimelech, a foundational text of the doctrine of the tzaddik. The doctrine of the tzaddik as the channel of divine flow (shefa) to the community is stated as his and the MOVEMENT'S attributed teaching, described and NOT affirmed or denied by the editor (neutrality #1, #4). The Hasidic-Mitnagdic conflict, including the mitnagdic objection to the elevation of the tzaddik, is given as historical CONTEXT and explicitly not adjudicated; the Lezajsk pilgrimage is recorded as the tradition's practice, not adjudicated. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-#9: (a) academic, Arthur Green, 'The Zaddiq as Axis Mundi in Later Judaism', Journal of the American Academy of Religion 45, no. 3 (1977): 327-347, and Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism, ninth lecture; (b) the tradition's own primary text, open and auditable on Sefaria, No'am Elimelech, with two passages read line-by-line (see below); (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar on-topic, Immanuel Etkes, 'The Zaddik: The Interrelationship between Religious Doctrine and Social Organization', in Hasidism Reappraised, ed. Ada Rapoport-Albert (Littman Library, 1996), 159-167. No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no YIVO Encyclopedia, no Chabad.org, no My Jewish Learning), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: No'am Elimelech on Sefaria is rated HIGH because two passages were READ line-by-line and confirmed verbatim in the open Sefaria Community Translation (CC0): (1) Parashat Bereshit, comment 1, the load-bearing statement of the tzaddik as channel of shefa, 'the complete clinging that the righteous have, through which they bring down the flow to all Israel, only good', and 'the righteous congregates the congregations of Yaakov that are collected under the shadow of the righteous' wings to bestow on them'; (2) Parashat Noach, comment 1, on the tzaddik's continual ascent 'from one aspect to another aspect' in serving God in all deeds. NOTE that the PRECISE CONTOURS of 'practical'/'popular' tzaddikism as a social-institutional doctrine (the tzaddik as intermediary shaping the rebbe institution) rest on the SECONDARY scholarship (Green, Etkes), not on a single line read in the primary No'am Elimelech text; that specific characterization is kept honest as attributed scholarship and is why this entry is left at status draft pending a reviewer's line-by-line confirmation of Green and Etkes. The secondary works (Green JAAR 1977; Scholem; Etkes) are medium, verified to exist and be on-topic (Oxford Academic/JSTOR for the Green article; Schocken/Princeton for Scholem; Littman Library / Liverpool University Press for the Etkes chapter), not read line-by-line. lifespan.note: 1717-1787 CE. Born Elimelech ben Elazar Lipman; a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch (d. 1772). With his brother Meshulam Zusha of Anipoli he carried Hasidism into Galicia and southern Poland, settling at Lezajsk (Lizhensk), where he died in 1787 and which became a site of pilgrimage associated with him.

relations.note: Elimelech was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, at whose court he studied and from which, with his brother Zusha and the other disciples, he went out to spread Hasidism into Galicia. sources.citation: Elimelech of Lizhensk. No'am Elimelech ('the Pleasantness of Elimelech'), commentary on the Torah. Open Hebrew and English text on Sefaria (Sefaria Community Translation, CC0). Cited as the openly-auditable primary text carrying Elimelech's own teaching, with two passages read line-by-line: (1) Sefer Bereshit, Parashat Bereshit, comment 1, the load-bearing statement of the doctrine of the tzaddik as channel of divine flow, 'the complete clinging that the righteous have, through which they bring down the flow to all Israel, only good', and 'the righteous congregates the congregations of Yaakov that are collected under the shadow of the righteous' wings to bestow on them'; (2) Sefer Bereshit, Parashat Noach, comment 1, on the tzaddik who serves God in all his deeds, 'even in physical things such as eating and drinking', and so 'always went from one aspect to another aspect'. These lines were read and verified verbatim as the load-bearing text for the doctrine of the tzaddik. The precise social-institutional contours of 'practical'/'popular' tzaddikism rest additionally on the secondary scholarship below.

sources.citation: Green, Arthur. 'The Zaddiq as Axis Mundi in Later Judaism.' Journal of the American Academy of Religion 45, no. 3 (September 1977): 327-347. A study tracing the notion of singular leadership and the place of the zaddiq in Jewish cosmology from rabbinic sources through the Hasidic masters, and the source most often cited for the theology of the tzaddik as cosmic pillar and intermediary that No'am Elimelech articulates; cited as the academic lens on the doctrine of the tzaddik. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Oxford Academic and JSTOR records, JAAR vol. XLV, no. 3), not read line-by-line.

Etkes, Immanuel. 'The Zaddik: The Interrelationship between Religious Doctrine and Social Organization.' In Hasidism Reappraised, edited by Ada Rapoport-Albert, 159-167. London: The Littman Library of Jewish Civilization, 1996. A contemporary Jewish scholar's study of how the religious doctrine of the tzaddik (formulated in works such as No'am Elimelech) connected to the social organization of Hasidic leadership, the emergence of the rebbe as an institution; cited as the contemporary-Jewish-scholarship lens on 'practical' tzaddikism and Elimelech's place in it. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Littman Library / Liverpool University Press record for Hasidism Reappraised), not read line-by-line.
